chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When the meal is placed, four thousand angels surround it. So when the servant says, “In the Name of Allah,” the angels say, “May Allah bless you in your meal.” Then they say to the Satan, “Exit, O mischievous one! You have no authority over them.”'
And when they finish and say, “All praise is for Allah,” the angels say, “A people upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, so they have fulfilled the gratitude of their Lord.”'
And if they do not say the Name (of Allah), the angels say to the Satan, “Approach, O mischievous one, so eat with them.”'
So when the meal is raised and they do not mention the Name of Allah upon it, the angels say, “A people upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, so they forgot their Lord, the Majestic and Mighty.”'

key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ: All praise is for Allah (the closing invocation)
key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ: In the Name of Allah (the opening invocation)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of saying Bismillah and Al-Hamdulillah before and after eating according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the metaphysical reality of dining, where the recitation of 'Bismillah' and 'Al-Hamdulillah' serves as a spiritual mechanism to invite divine blessings and expel Satan, who is depicted as a literal consumer of the meal when the name is omitted. Scholars highlight this as a practical application of the concept of *shukr* (gratitude), linking the physical act of eating to the spiritual state of remembrance (*dhikr*). The narration underscores the continuous presence of angels and Satan in daily life, making the meal a microcosm of the cosmic struggle between divine favor and satanic influence.
